quick_revision.title: Electric Current and Circuit Laws (Quick Revision)
quick_revision.definition: The rate of flow of electric charge is called electric current. Ohm's and Kirchhoff's laws are the basic foundation for circuit analysis.
quick_revision.explanation: Electric current (I) = Q/t. The relation between potential difference and current in a conductor is given by Ohm's law, while Kirchhoff's junction and loop rules are used to solve complex electric circuits.
importantPoints: Electric current: I = Q/t (Unit: Ampere)
Ohm's law: V = IR
Resistance: R = V/I (Unit: Ohm)
Specific resistance (Resistivity): ρ = RA/l (Unit: Ohm-meter)
Kirchhoff's junction rule (Conservation of charge): ΣI = 0
Kirchhoff's loop rule (Conservation of energy): ΣV = 0

questions.explanation:
Formula : I = Q / t
SI Unit - Ampere (A)

questions.explanation:

quick_revision.title: Magnetic Dipole and Classification of Materials (Quick Revision)
quick_revision.definition: Based on magnetic behavior, materials are classified into diamagnetic, paramagnetic, and ferromagnetic categories.
quick_revision.explanation: Magnetic dipole moment is the product of pole strength and the distance between the two poles. Magnetic field lines form closed loops and never intersect each other.
importantPoints: Magnetic dipole moment: M = m × 2l (Unit: Ampere-meter²)
Diamagnetic: Weakly repelled by magnetic field (e.g., Bismuth, Copper, Water)
Paramagnetic: Weakly attracted towards magnetic field (e.g., Aluminium, Oxygen)
Ferromagnetic: Strongly attracted towards magnetic field (e.g., Iron, Cobalt, Nickel)
Magnetic field lines never intersect each other

quick_revision.title: Alternating Circuits and Devices (Quick Revision)
quick_revision.definition: A current whose magnitude and direction change periodically with time is called Alternating Current (AC).
quick_revision.explanation: In AC circuits, the RMS value of current is the effective value. Power factor determines energy loss, and a transformer changes voltage through mutual induction.
importantPoints: Instantaneous value: I = I₀ sin ωt
RMS value: Irms = I₀ / √2
Power factor: cos φ = R / Z
Resonance condition: XL = XC
Resonant frequency: f₀ = 1 / (2π√LC)
Transformer ratio: Vs / Vp = Ns / Np (Mutual Induction)

quick_revision.title: Electromagnetic Waves and Spectrum (Quick Revision)
quick_revision.definition: Waves produced by the propagation of mutually perpendicular oscillating electric and magnetic fields are called Electromagnetic Waves.
quick_revision.explanation: These are transverse waves that travel in vacuum with the speed of light (3 × 10⁸ m/s). They do not require any material medium for propagation.
importantPoints: Electric and magnetic fields oscillate perpendicular to each other
Speed in vacuum: c = 1 / √(μ₀ε₀) = 3 × 10⁸ m/s
Spectrum order: Radio, Micro, Infrared, Visible, Ultraviolet, X-rays, Gamma rays
Ultraviolet rays: Used in sterilization and detecting forged documents

quick_revision.title: Optics Laws and Optical Instruments (Quick Revision)
quick_revision.definition: The study of reflection, refraction of light, and working principles of various optical instruments (such as microscope) is called Ray Optics.
quick_revision.explanation: Total internal reflection occurs when angle of incidence is greater than critical angle. Power of a lens is equal to the reciprocal of its focal length, and lenses are designed using the Lens Maker's formula.
importantPoints: Total internal reflection: Denser to rarer medium, i > C
Critical angle relation: sin C = 1 / μ
Power of lens: P = 1 / f (in meters), Unit: Dioptre (D)
Lens maker's formula: 1/f = (μ - 1)(1/R₁ - 1/R₂)
Compound microscope: High magnification using objective and eyepiece lenses

quick_revision.title: Wave Theory and Optical Phenomena (Quick Revision)
quick_revision.definition: Considering light as a wave, the study of phenomena like interference, diffraction, and polarization is called Wave Optics.
quick_revision.explanation: According to Huygens, every point on a wavefront is a source of secondary wavelets. Interference is related to superposition of waves, diffraction to bending around corners, and polarization to transverse nature of light.
importantPoints: Wavefront: Surface of particles vibrating in the same phase
Huygens' principle: Each point is a source of secondary wavelets
Interference: Change in intensity due to superposition of waves
Diffraction: Bending of light around corners of obstacle or aperture
Polarization: Restricting vibrations of light to one fixed direction (proof of transverse nature)

quick_revision.title: Photoelectric Effect and de Broglie Waves (Quick Revision)
quick_revision.definition: Radiation energy shows both particle and wave behavior, which is called the dual nature of radiation and matter.
quick_revision.explanation: The emission of electrons from a metal surface by light of suitable frequency is the photoelectric effect, which was explained by Einstein. de Broglie stated that a wave is associated with every moving particle.
importantPoints: Work function: Minimum energy required to free an electron from a metal surface
Threshold frequency: Minimum frequency required for electron emission
de Broglie formula: λ = h / p = h / (mv)
Einstein's equation: hν = φ + Kmax = φ + 1/2 mv²max

quick_revision.title: Atomic Models and Energy Levels (Quick Revision)
quick_revision.definition: Rutherford's nuclear model and Bohr's quantum model were proposed to explain atomic structure.
quick_revision.explanation: Rutherford discovered the heavy nucleus at the center, while Bohr gave the concept of fixed non-radiating stationary orbits and energy quantization.
importantPoints: Rutherford model: Tiny positively charged nucleus at center, most part is empty
Bohr model: Non-radiating stationary orbits with fixed energy
Ionization energy: Minimum energy required to take an electron from ground state to infinity
Excitation energy: Energy required to move an electron from ground state to a higher energy state
Energy formula: En = - 13.6 / n² eV

quick_revision.title: Nuclear Composition and Radioactivity (Quick Revision)
quick_revision.definition: The central dense positively charged part of an atom is called the nucleus, in which protons and neutrons are bound together.
quick_revision.explanation: The difference between the mass of constituent nucleons and the actual mass of the nucleus is called mass defect, which becomes binding energy by Einstein's relation (E=Δmc²). Unstable nuclei exhibit radioactivity.
importantPoints: Nuclear composition: Protons + Neutrons (Nucleons)
Mass defect: Total mass of free nucleons - Actual mass of nucleus
Binding energy: Minimum energy required to separate nucleons from each other
Radioactivity: Spontaneous emission of α, β, γ radiations from unstable nuclei
Half-life formula: Remaining nuclei after one half-life N = N₀ / 2

quick_revision.title: Semiconductors and Diode Devices (Quick Revision)
quick_revision.definition: Materials whose conductivity lies between conductors and insulators are called Semiconductors.
quick_revision.explanation: Adding impurities (doping) forms P-type (trivalent impurity) and N-type (pentavalent impurity) semiconductors. Joining them forms a P-N junction diode, which is used in rectification.
importantPoints: Semiconductor: Conductivity between conductor and insulator (e.g., Silicon, Germanium)
Pure (Intrinsic) semiconductor: Internal semiconductor without any impurity
P-type: Trivalent impurity, majority carriers: Holes
N-type: Pentavalent impurity, majority carriers: Electrons
P-N junction diode: Mainly used to convert AC into DC (Rectifier)

questions.explanation: Examples : Silicon and Germanium.
